why: The property nothing found provides is graceful DEGRADATION of a secret-bearing file into a still-useful manifest entry: snap.py records its sha256 so drift stays detectable, never writes its bytes into the snapshot, and then makes restore REFUSE to claim success over it (snap.py:400-433 prints CANNOT and returns 1). Every alternative resolves the same tension a different way -- chezmoi and yadm ENCRYPT the secret and carry it into git history anyway, Claude Vault REDACTS by mutating the file so what you restore is not what you backed up, gitleaks in a hook REFUSES the whole operation, and AIDE/mtree record hashes for everything and can restore nothing. The second property is the manifest/content split enforced by state/snapshots/.gitignore (`*/files/`), which makes the tabular half plaintext and reviewable in a PR diff while the bytes stay off this machine's git history; restic's index is inside an encrypted repository, so you cannot read what a snapshot captured without the repo and its password. The third is verify's policy half (snap.py:302-358): NOWDENIED re-evaluates an OLD snapshot's entries against the CURRENT deny lists, asking whether a snapshot taken under looser policy is still allowed to hold what it holds -- FIM tools ask the opposite question (does the filesystem still match the baseline) and never re-judge the baseline against newer policy. I will not pretend the margin is wide: chezmoi with a .chezmoiignore allowlist, run on Windows, would cover capture, diff-against-live, apply/restore and git history, and its remaining gaps (no per-take id, no hash-only degradation, no policy recheck, secrets encrypted-in-git rather than absent) are a design disagreement plus roughly 100 lines, not a chasm. What keeps the verdict here is that ~/.claude is already written by tools/deploy and by sync-live-settings.py, so handing chezmoi ownership of the desired state of a tree two other things mutate replaces a 380-line undo with a second control plane and a merge problem.

alternatives.name: chezmoi (chezmoi.io, twpayne/chezmoi, Go binary)
alternatives.covers: genuinely the closest fit and the strongest candidate here: cross-platform including Windows, physically copies files rather than symlinking, `chezmoi diff` shows what apply would change in the home directory and `chezmoi status` summarises it (verified from chezmoi.io/reference/commands/diff and /status), `.chezmoiignore` gives the exclusion list (verified from chezmoi.io/reference/special-files/chezmoiignore: 'interpreted as a set of patterns to ignore', matched against the target path), and git history of the source directory gives versioning and rollback
alternatives.gap: it is a DESIRED-STATE manager with exactly one source state, not a point-in-time ledger: there is no `take` that stamps an id you can name later, so 'snapshot the live tree right now before deploy touches it' means committing to the source repo, and two takes in one second (the exact defect snap.py:197-210 exists to prevent) has no analogue. Its answer to secrets is age/gpg ENCRYPTION into the git repo, which is the specific thing snap.py:16-19 refuses -- and the chezmoiignore docs I fetched do NOT state that ignoring a file prevents it entering the source state, only that it controls what is applied, so an allowlist posture there needs verifying before trusting. No verify-snapshot-against-its-own-manifest, no re-check of an old capture against current policy, and apply CAN remove files from the destination, where snap.py has no delete code path at all (snap.py:415-417 names appeared-later files and leaves them).
alternatives.cost: single Go binary, free/open source (licence not verified this session), no runtime daemon; migration cost is re-expressing INCLUDE_FILES/INCLUDE_TREES/DENY_* as chezmoiignore patterns and accepting a second owner of ~/.claude alongside tools/deploy
alternatives.maturity: clearly active: 2026 blog posts and open GitHub issues (#4180 on status output, #2033 on Windows symlink status) found this session. Release cadence, star count and licence NOT verified.

alternatives.name: restic / borg / kopia (content-addressed snapshot backup, restic.readthedocs.io)
alternatives.covers: the snapshot half properly: per-snapshot ids that can never collide, deduplicated content store, `restic restore --dry-run` (verified in the 0.19.1 stable restore docs I fetched), `--overwrite never`, and `restic check --read-data` which verifies pack-file integrity -- that is a strictly better-engineered version of cmd_verify's integrity half (snap.py:327-341)
alternatives.gap: no secret awareness of any kind: a file is either excluded by pattern or stored in full, so the hash-only middle state that keeps drift detectable without carrying bytes does not exist and cannot be expressed. The repository is encrypted and opaque, so the manifest cannot be git-tracked, reviewed in a PR, or read from a fresh clone -- which is the whole point of the split at state/snapshots/.gitignore. `restic restore --delete` DOES remove files absent from the snapshot (verified in the same docs), so 'never deletes' becomes a flag you must remember rather than a property of the code. No policy re-check (NOWDENIED), no orphan detection against a declared entry list, no reason strings explaining why a path was excluded.
alternatives.cost: a Go binary plus a repository plus a password/keyfile to manage, to replace two shutil.copy2 calls (snap.py:241 and snap.py:430). That is the whole content-store surface here -- roughly 5 lines of the 826.
alternatives.maturity: restic docs served as 0.19.1 stable / 0.19.1-dev latest at the pages I fetched on 2026-07-29, so it is actively released. borg and kopia were seen only in third-party comparison articles this session, not verified from their own release pages.

alternatives.name: AIDE / Tripwire / osquery FIM (file integrity monitoring)
alternatives.covers: the manifest-and-hash drift half exactly: build a sha256 baseline of a tree, re-scan later, report added/changed/removed. This is precisely cmd_diff (snap.py:384-397) and it is what these tools have done since 1992, with far more attention to metadata (permissions, inode, mtime) than snap.py's path/size/sha256
alternatives.gap: detection only -- none of them stores content, so there is no restore and never was; AIDE is hash-only for EVERYTHING, which is the degraded state snap.py reserves for secret-bearing files. No secret-pattern classification, no reason string per excluded path, no snapshot id or ledger of takes. AIDE and Tripwire's open-source line are Linux-oriented and this machine is Windows 11; osquery is cross-platform but is a daemon with a SQL interface, which is a wildly disproportionate install for one 826-line local undo. None re-judges an old baseline against a newer policy.
alternatives.cost: AIDE/Tripwire: package install plus a policy file plus a baseline DB, Linux-first. osquery: an agent process on the machine permanently.
alternatives.maturity: all long-established (Tripwire dates to 1992 per the Tripwire buyer's guide found this session; osquery FIM documented at osquery.readthedocs.io). Current release versions and Windows FIM parity NOT verified this session.

alternatives.name: mtree / go-mtree (BSD mtree(8), vbatts/go-mtree)
alternatives.covers: the manifest FORMAT and its verification, as a standard rather than a bespoke JSON schema: `mtree -c -K sha256digest` writes a textual spec of a hierarchy, and re-running against the spec reports every path that does not match, exiting 2 on mismatch (verified from man.openbsd.org/mtree.8 and the mankier mtree(5) format page). go-mtree gives the same thing as a cross-platform Go binary and library, so Windows is covered
alternatives.gap: it maps and verifies a hierarchy; it does not copy content, so restore does not exist. No include/deny classification with a per-path reason, no secret scanning, no snapshot ids, no pre-restore safety take. Adopting it would replace manifest.json's shape (snap.py:245-256) with a standard format and buy interoperability, but every behaviour the WHY-THIS-EXISTS docstring names would still be hand-written around it.
alternatives.cost: free; go-mtree is a Go binary/library, BSD mtree is not present on Windows. Migration would mean writing an mtree spec emitter plus a parser to keep the captured/reason fields, which the format has no native slot for.
alternatives.maturity: go-mtree tag v0.4.2 visible in the GitHub search results; whether that is current or the project is actively maintained in 2026 was NOT verified.

alternatives.name: etckeeper (etckeeper.branchable.com)
alternatives.covers: the closest philosophical sibling: version-control a live config directory that other processes write into, auto-commit before and after those writes, and roll back with a git checkout of a path at a commit. It also tracks metadata git cannot (file permissions), which snap.py's manifest does not record at all
alternatives.gap: its whole model is 'put the config tree in git', including secrets -- its documented answer for /etc/shadow is permission tracking plus keeping the repo private, which is exactly the posture snap.py:16-19 rejects on the grounds that a later delete does not remove a blob from history. Linux and package-manager oriented (apt/yum/pacman hooks), no Windows support found. No hash-only degradation, no allowlist-with-reasons, no verification of a past commit against current policy.
alternatives.cost: free, Linux package; would require the ~/.claude tree to become a git repository, which collides with the credential files sitting at its top level (.credentials.json, .setup-token-tmp, .token-flow/ are all present on this machine, confirmed by listing names only).
alternatives.maturity: long-established, still written about in 2026 (oneuptime.com 2026-03-02 post found this session). Upstream release activity NOT verified.

alternatives.name: gitleaks (github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) / detect-secrets
alternatives.covers: the slice this component is weakest at: SECRET_PATTERNS (snap.py:103-114) is 10 hand-written regexes, and gitleaks maintains a community ruleset far larger than that. It scans plain directories and individual files outside git history, and `--redact` keeps the matched value out of logs and stdout -- which is the same constraint secret_reason() enforces at snap.py:125-139 by returning the pattern NAME and never the match
alternatives.gap: it is a detector, not a capture/restore tool: no manifest, no content store, no diff-against-live, no restore. Integrating it means shelling out per take and parsing a JSON report to get the per-file boolean that entry_for() needs (snap.py:185-194), which turns a pure-stdlib in-process byte scan into a subprocess plus report parse plus a redaction flag you must not forget. It also cannot express the hash-only outcome; its verbs are report and block.
alternatives.cost: a Go binary that must be present offline on Windows, added to a currently zero-dependency stdlib tool, in exchange for a better regex table.
alternatives.maturity: actively maintained and widely packaged (Kali packages it; a 2026-01-25 oneuptime post documents current usage) -- established from third-party pages, NOT from its own release feed this session.

alternatives.name: claude-code-backup (github.com/mcpware/claude-code-backup) and Claude Vault (claudevault.vercel.app)
alternatives.covers: purpose-built for this exact tree, and each covers ground snap.py deliberately or accidentally does not. claude-code-backup scans everything Claude Code stores across the machine -- memories, skills, MCP configs, rules, CLAUDE.md, settings, plans, sessions, plugins -- on a 4-hour schedule. Claude Vault snapshots ~/.claude and ~/.agents to a GitHub repo, redacts settings.json before pushing and REFUSES TO COMMIT if redaction cannot run cleanly, and on restore moves the current ~/.claude aside to a timestamped directory first, which is the same instinct as snap.py:425's pre-restore take
alternatives.gap: claude-code-backup: its README (fetched 2026-07-29) does not mention secret exclusion at all and its stated mitigation is 'keep the backup repo private' -- the posture snap.py refuses; restore is manual with 'automated restore coming soon'; no diff against live, no integrity verify, no snapshot ids. Claude Vault: macOS 15+ only, so it cannot run on this Windows 11 machine at all; it redacts by MUTATING content, so a restored settings.json is not the file that was backed up -- snap.py's hash-only entry is honest about not being restorable instead of silently returning a different file; open-source status not stated. Both push to GitHub, so neither is an offline local undo.
alternatives.cost: claude-code-backup needs Node 18+, git and a private GitHub repo (network dependency). Claude Vault is a free ~5MB macOS binary, unusable here.
alternatives.maturity: both exist and were fetched this session; claude-code-backup's page shows a 2026 footer with no explicit release date, Claude Vault gives no version or licence. Commit activity, licence and download counts NOT verified for either.

alternatives.name: git-annex (git-annex.branchable.com) / DVC (dvc.org)
alternatives.covers: the structural pattern this component's design rests on -- keep metadata in git, keep content out of it, addressed by hash. git-annex checks in a pointer while the bytes live in a key-value store; DVC's .dvc pointer files are always in git while the data sits on a remote. That is state/snapshots/.gitignore's `*/files/` split, done by a maintained tool with location tracking and integrity checks
alternatives.gap: both are built for large data files and ML workflows, not for a 128-entry config tree of small text files, and both want a remote to be useful. Neither classifies content: nothing decides that a file is secret-bearing and must become metadata-only, which is the entire point of the split here (in ours the split is per-file and content-driven, in theirs it is per-repo and size-driven). No restore-to-an-arbitrary-live-tree semantics, no policy re-check, no dry-run-that-names-what-it-will-not-write.
alternatives.cost: git-annex is a Haskell binary with a rough Windows story (not verified this session, but long-reported); DVC is a Python package that expects a remote. Either is a large conceptual dependency for one local undo.
alternatives.maturity: both long-established with current manpages/docs (Debian unstable git-annex manpage, dvc.org user guide, both seen this session). Release cadence NOT verified.

evidence: Read tools/snapshot/snap.py in full, all 826 lines, single file, no other .py in the directory (confirmed by ls: only snap.py and __pycache__/). Read docs/prior-art/tools-gate.json in full as the depth template. Read state/snapshots/.gitignore (3-sentence rationale plus the single pattern `*/files/`). Inspected the one real snapshot on disk, state/snapshots/20260725T110903Z-pre-bus-wiring/manifest.json: schema 1, 128 entries, 128 captured, 0 hash-only, skipped_count 21, 23 not_walked directories. Listed ~/.claude top-level NAMES ONLY (no file contents read, no credential file opened) to check the include list against the live tree. Confirmed via `git ls-files state/snapshots` that the manifest is tracked and the files/ half is not. Searches run 2026-07-29: dotfiles managers with snapshot/restore and secret handling (chezmoi/yadm/stow); file integrity monitoring with sha256 baselines (AIDE/Tripwire/osquery); restic-vs-borg-vs-kopia dry-run and exclude semantics; backup tools that skip or redact secret-bearing files (gitleaks/detect-secrets); mtree hierarchy manifests with sha256digest; etckeeper for version-controlled live config; chezmoi Windows support and diff/status; git-annex and DVC metadata-in-git patterns; and a targeted search for tools purpose-built to back up ~/.claude. Pages fetched: restic stable restore docs (confirmed --dry-run, --delete, and the four --overwrite modes verbatim), chezmoi .chezmoiignore reference, the claude-code-backup GitHub page, and claudevault.vercel.app. NOT VERIFIED: I installed and ran none of these tools, so every claim about what they would cost to migrate to is an estimate from reading. I did not run `snap.py selftest` this session, so the 354-line selftest is read but not executed evidence. I did not verify licences, release cadences, star counts, or Windows binary availability for chezmoi, gitleaks, go-mtree, borg, kopia, git-annex or DVC. I did not verify whether .chezmoiignore prevents a file entering chezmoi's SOURCE state or only its application -- the doc page I fetched does not say, and that distinction decides whether chezmoi can hold an allowlist posture at all. I did not check whether any of the two purpose-built Claude Code backup tools is maintained beyond the pages existing.
recheck: Run: `python C:/Users/shova/claude-setup/tools/snapshot/snap.py selftest` (must stay green before any migration is even discussed), then `gh release list --repo twpayne/chezmoi --limit 5`, `gh release list --repo restic/restic --limit 5`, `gh release list --repo mcpware/claude-code-backup --limit 5`, and `gh api repos/vbatts/go-mtree --jq .pushed_at`. Then WebSearch "chezmoi snapshot point-in-time id restore previous apply" and "restic backup skip file containing secret hash only manifest". RE-OPEN THIS VERDICT IF any of: (a) chezmoi ships a per-apply snapshot id with a restore-to-that-id command, (b) any backup tool documents recording a file as hash-only-because-secret-bearing rather than encrypting or excluding it, (c) claude-code-backup ships automated restore plus documented credential exclusion and is cross-platform, or (d) `python -c "import json;m=json.load(open('state/snapshots/<newest>/manifest.json'));print(m['skipped_count'], m['not_walked'])"` shows the skipped/not-walked set growing past the point where the allowlist is still an honest description of the live tree.
what_ours_does: One file, snap.py, 826 lines, stdlib only, five subcommands plus a selftest. It exists because the only undo for tools/deploy and sync-live-settings.py was a single fixed-name .bak copy that destroyed its own pristine copy on the second run (snap.py:2-14). take (snap.py:224-271) walks ~/.claude through an ALLOWLIST -- five named top-level files (snap.py:68-74) and seven named directories (snap.py:78-80) -- while classify (snap.py:142-157) applies three deny sets that WIN over the allowlist: names, path parts, suffixes (snap.py:85-97). candidates (snap.py:160-182) deliberately offers every top-level file including .credentials.json to classify so the deny branches are exercised by real input rather than sitting untested. Any file whose raw BYTES match one of ten secret patterns (snap.py:103-114) becomes a hash-only entry: sha256 in the manifest, content never copied (snap.py:185-194, snap.py:238-243), and secret_reason (snap.py:125-139) returns the pattern NAME never the match, because the reason string is written into a git-tracked file. new_id (snap.py:197-210) stamps a UTC id per take with a collision loop, and do_take's mkdir uses exist_ok=False as a second guard behind it. The output splits along a git boundary enforced by state/snapshots/.gitignore (`*/files/`): content local and gitignored, manifest.json tracked. verify (snap.py:302-358) checks two things -- integrity (MISSING, CHANGED, and LEAKED for a hash-only entry whose content somehow exists) and POLICY against the bytes on disk (ORPHAN for content the manifest never mentions, NOWDENIED for an entry the CURRENT deny lists would refuse, SECRET for a captured file matching a pattern on re-scan). diff (snap.py:361-397) compares the live tree to a manifest alone, with --fail-on-drift for a verifier, and a hash-only entry stays comparable because its hash was recorded. restore (snap.py:400-433) is a dry run by default, takes a pre-restore snapshot before writing so the restore is itself revertable (snap.py:425), never deletes a file that appeared after the snapshot but names it LEFT (snap.py:415-417), and returns 1 with CANNOT rather than claiming success over a hash-only entry (snap.py:412-414, 433). selftest (snap.py:436-789, ~354 lines, 43% of the file) plants a fake live tree and asserts each property, including denied names and dirs NESTED inside allowlisted trees so the deny branches are actually reachable (snap.py:504-516), a stubbed new_id to force the unreachable exist_ok=False guard under test (snap.py:640-653), a hand-built policy-drift fixture that no current take could produce (snap.py:690-702), and crash-as-verdict wrappers around take and every command (snap.py:471-486, 562-575) because an escaping exception reads to the mutation harness as 'caught' with no check naming the reason.
strongest_counterargument: The defended properties are load-bearing only if the allowlist is an honest description of the live tree, and on this machine right now it is not. The one real snapshot captured 128 files, recorded 0 hash-only entries -- so the secret-degradation machinery that this whole verdict rests on has NEVER FIRED in production -- and silently skipped 21 top-level files and 23 directories. Listing ~/.claude confirms what is missing: keybindings.json, SHORTCUTS.md, scheduled_tasks.json, config/, plans/, docs/, tasks/ and jobs/ are all live configuration and none is on INCLUDE_FILES or INCLUDE_TREES, while INCLUDE_TREES still lists output-styles, which does not exist. Worse, the manifest records not_walked by NAME but skipped files only as skipped_count (snap.py:245-254), so from the git-tracked half -- the half the design says proves the shape of the tree -- a future reader cannot learn WHICH 21 files were left out. The docstring's claim that coverage is never overstated is true of the terminal output and false of the artifact. A tool that has captured no secret, skips a quarter of the live top-level config, and cannot tell you what it skipped is a tool whose unique properties are theoretical, and claude-code-backup and Claude Vault -- both purpose-built for this exact tree, both found in one search -- explicitly cover the sessions, plans and plugins that this one does not. The second cut is duplication: SECRET_PATTERNS (snap.py:103-114) is a second hand-rolled secret regex table in a repo that already has one in gate.py, and the tools-gate record defends that one on the same 'no off-the-shelf equivalent' grounds while gitleaks maintains a far larger ruleset than either. Two bespoke scanners defended by two prior-art records citing each other's absence is the shape a rubber stamp takes. The most honest reading is that this component earns 'keep-ours' on its restore semantics and its selftest, not on its classifier -- and that the correct next action is not to defend it but to fix the include list, name the skipped files in the manifest, and cross-check both regex tables against gitleaks' rules.
